client: I got a rejection letter from my dream university last week, and honestly it's been really hard to shake off. I keep thinking that maybe I was never good enough to begin with, and that this just proves it. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything — it happened, the letter is real, and I don't see how sitting here is going to make me feel less like a failure.
therapist: That rejection clearly hit somewhere deep, and the thought that it "proves" you were never good enough is such a painful place to land — but I want to gently push back on that, because one decision from one admissions committee can't actually measure your worth or your potential. Even as you're saying you're not sure this will help, I notice you're here and talking about it, which tells me part of you is still looking for a way through this — what would it mean for you if that thought, "I was never good enough," turned out not to be true?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... if that thought turned out not to be true, I guess it would be a relief, but honestly it almost feels scarier than just accepting it. Like, if I'm not "never good enough," then what does that rejection even mean? I don't know how to make sense of it without that explanation, even if the explanation hurts.
therapist: What you just said is really profound — that the painful explanation feels *safer* than uncertainty, because at least it gives you a story to hold onto. That's actually a very human thing to do; our minds would rather have a harsh answer than no answer at all. So I'm curious — if the rejection didn't mean you're not good enough, what are some other explanations, even small or partial ones, that might also be true?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... I guess there could be other reasons. Like maybe the timing was just off, or they were already talking to someone else, or they just weren't in a place to connect with anyone new right now. But honestly, when I try to think those thoughts, they feel kind of hollow, like I'm just making excuses for myself rather than actually believing them.
therapist: It's really interesting that you can actually generate those alternative explanations — your mind *can* go there — but something about them feels like they don't quite land yet. I wonder if they feel hollow not because they're untrue, but because you've been holding the "not good enough" story for longer, so it just has more weight and familiarity right now. What would it take for one of those other explanations to feel even a little more real to you, rather than like an excuse?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I think you're right that the "not good enough" story has been around a lot longer... it's like it's worn a groove in my brain and the other explanations feel like they're just sitting on the surface. For one of them to feel real, I think I'd need some kind of actual evidence, not just logic — like, I'd need to experience someone actually wanting to spend time with me without me having to earn it or prove something first. But honestly, even saying that out loud, part of me is already bracing for why that won't happen.
therapist: You just named something really important — that what you need isn't more logic, but an *experience* of being wanted without having to earn it, and that's a deeply human need, not a weakness. But I'm also noticing that even as you articulated that so clearly, you immediately moved to protect yourself from hoping for it — like part of you is already building a wall before anything has even happened. What do you think that part of you is trying to protect you from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I think that part of me is trying to protect me from getting hurt again — like, if I don't let myself hope for it, then I can't be disappointed when it doesn't happen. It's almost like I've been let down so many times that hoping feels more dangerous than just staying numb to it. But hearing you say it out loud like that... I don't know, it's a little unsettling because I can see that the wall is there, I just don't know if I actually want to take it down.
therapist: The honesty in what you just said is really striking — you can *see* the wall, and you're not even sure you want it gone, because it's been keeping you safe for a long time. That ambivalence makes complete sense; taking down a protection that's worked, even imperfectly, feels like a real risk. I'm curious — when you imagine a version of you who didn't need that wall quite so high, what does that person's life look like?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess that person... they'd actually pick up the phone when a friend calls instead of letting it go to voicemail and then feeling guilty about it for three days. They'd maybe go to that dinner party without spending the whole night feeling like everyone's just tolerating them being there. But honestly, even picturing that feels kind of naive, like I'm describing someone who just hasn't been hurt enough yet to know better.
therapist: You painted a really vivid and specific picture just then — answering the phone, being at that dinner without the dread — and those details tell me that version of you isn't as abstract or naive as you're making it sound, because you can *see* it clearly. And I notice there's something a little tender in the way you described it, like you're both drawn to that life and already grieving it as impossible. What would it mean to hold onto that picture just a little longer, without immediately dismissing it as naivety?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I guess it would mean... letting myself want something I'm not sure I can have, and that's actually scarier than just writing it off as impossible. If I hold onto it and then it doesn't happen, I've lost something twice — once in reality, and once in my imagination. It's like I've already learned that hoping too hard just makes the disappointment worse.
therapist: What you just described — losing something twice, once in reality and once in your imagination — is such an honest and painful way to live, and it makes complete sense that hoping has come to feel like a setup rather than a gift. But I want to sit with something you said: you've *learned* that hoping makes disappointment worse, which means that's a conclusion drawn from real experiences of being hurt, not just a fact about how the world works. I'm wondering — has there ever been a time, even a small one, where you hoped for something and it didn't destroy you when it didn't go perfectly?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I have to think about that for a second, because my instinct is to say no, but... there was this one time I applied for a small grant for a project I was working on, and I let myself get a little excited about it, and when I didn't get it I was disappointed but I kept going. But I don't know if that really counts, because the stakes felt lower somehow, like I hadn't fully let myself hope the way I do with people. When it comes to actual relationships or people I care about, it feels completely different, like the hoping goes so much deeper that there's no safe version of it.
therapist: You actually found it — and I don't want to let that slip by, because your instinct was to say no, but you went looking anyway and came back with something real. What strikes me is that you *did* let yourself hope for that grant, and when it didn't work out, something in you kept moving forward — which suggests the hoping didn't break you, even if it hurt. I'm curious about this distinction you're drawing, though — what is it about people specifically that makes the hoping feel so much more dangerous than anything else?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think it's because when a grant falls through, it's just... circumstances, you know? It's not personal. But when I let myself hope that someone actually wants to be close to me, and then they drift away or don't show up the way I needed, it feels like proof that there's something fundamentally wrong with me, not just bad luck.
therapist: You've just named the heart of it — that with people, disappointment doesn't feel like bad luck, it feels like a verdict about who you are. That's such a heavy thing to carry, where every time someone doesn't show up, it becomes more evidence for a case that's already been building for a long time. I'm wondering — who first taught you that when people leave or let you down, it means something is wrong with *you* rather than with the circumstances or even just with them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I've never really thought about it that way before, like there being a specific person who taught me that. But honestly, I think it was my mom — she had this way of making everything feel like a reflection of her, and when she was disappointed in me, it wasn't just about what I did, it was like I was fundamentally flawed somehow. I guess I just... absorbed that, and now it's like that voice is just mine.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really significant — that the voice telling you you're fundamentally flawed wasn't born inside you, it was handed to you by someone who needed you to reflect her, and that's not the same as truth. It makes so much sense that it feels like your own voice now, because you've been carrying it for so long, but there's something important in recognizing it had an origin outside of you. I'm curious — when you hear that critical voice now, does it ever sound like her, or has it become so familiar that it just sounds like you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
